screens.title: Understanding the Hardhat Project Structure
screens.subtitle: A clear mental model for contracts, scripts, tests, and configuration

narration.text: In this chapter we map a typical Hardhat project so you always know where code, tests, and deployment logic belong. You will learn the role of contracts, scripts, tests, and the central hardhat. config. js file. We’ll also cover the package manifest, the dependency folder, and the compilation outputs that your frontend or deployment tools rely on. Knowing this layout speeds development, reduces errors when compiling or deploying, and makes collaboration predictable. For example, when someone adds a new Solidity file under contracts, Hardhat’s compiler discovers it automatically. Later you’ll inspect the artifacts folder to see the contract ABI and bytecode that your frontend will use. We’ll highlight common pitfalls too, such as accidentally committing node_modules or mismatching the Solidity version. By the end you’ll be able to navigate a repository, update configuration safely, and know which files to share with teammates. What part of the project layout feels most uncertain to you right now?

keyIdea.text: A predictable Hardhat structure helps compilers, tests, and deployment scripts work together and keeps collaboration friction low.

screens.title: Bloom's Progression
screens.subtitle: From naming files to configuring deployable builds

narration.text: This short progression shows how you move from basic recognition to practical mastery. First you learn to name and find key directories so you can open and edit the right files. Next you understand what each file does, for example that artifacts includes ABI and bytecode used by frontends. Then you apply that knowledge by editing hardhat. config. js and running a compile or a deployment script. Finally you master consistent team workflows by committing only source and lockfiles, and ensuring the Solidity version and optimizer settings match your contracts. Each stage connects to a hands-on action: opening contracts, running npx hardhat compile, running tests, or making a small configuration change and observing the outcome. A common misconception is thinking node_modules must be shared; instead you commit package-lock. json and allow teammates to restore node_modules locally. Practicing these steps builds reliable development and deployment habits.

keyIdea.text: Move from recognizing files to editing configuration and verifying builds to achieve repeatable team workflows.

screens.title: The contracts/ directory
screens.subtitle: Where Solidity source files live and why organization matters

narration.text: The contracts directory is the canonical location for all your Solidity source files. Hardhat’s compiler looks here by default, so placing MyToken. sol, Greeter. sol, or other contracts in contracts means they’ll be discovered and compiled automatically. For larger projects it’s common to add subdirectories, for example contracts/tokens or contracts/governance, which helps developers quickly find related code. A concrete example from the sample project is Greeter. sol — when saved under contracts and compiled, Hardhat produces an artifacts JSON for Greeter that includes the ABI and bytecode. A frequent misconception is that files can be scattered anywhere; while you can change paths via configuration, doing so requires updating hardhat. config. js and risks confusion for teammates. Another practical point: keep source contracts separate from generated outputs — never edit compiled files. As a quick rule, treat contracts/ as input source that you author and version in Git. The key takeaway is a simple one: place Solidity source in contracts and adopt a folder naming convention early to avoid entanglement as the project grows. The contracts/ directory means put all .sol files here and organize with subfolders to keep related contracts grouped for readability and maintenance.. In practical terms, where solidity source files live and why organization matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Core Concept The contracts/ directory
The contracts/ directory
Where your Solidity source is authored and stored for compilation.
Definition & purpose
All Solidity (.sol) files go here by default. Hardhat compiles these files and produces artifacts used by deployment scripts and frontends.
Best practices
  • Organize by feature, e.g., contracts/tokens or contracts/governance.
  • Keep source files under version control; do not include generated artifacts.
  • Make sure pragma lines are compatible with your configured compiler version.
Key Takeaway

Treat contracts/ as the single source of truth for Solidity code. Use subfolders early to avoid clutter.

Concrete example
The sample project includes Greeter.sol in contracts. When compiled, Hardhat generates Greeter.json in artifacts with ABI and bytecode so scripts and frontends can interact with the contract.
Common misconception
You might think you can keep .sol anywhere. While possible, moving sources requires path configuration and confuses other developers unless documented.

screens.title: The scripts/ directory and deploy workflow
screens.subtitle: Write, run, and reuse deployment and utility scripts

narration.text: Scripts are JavaScript or TypeScript files that perform tasks such as deploying contracts, running administrative actions, or seeding data. The scripts/ folder is the conventional place to store these files. A typical flow is: write a deploy script that imports a compiled contract factory, deploys the contract, and logs the deployed address; run it with npx hardhat run scripts/deploy. js --network sepolia or without --network to use the Hardhat Network. The sample project includes a deploy. js that demonstrates basic deployment logic. Scripts provide repeatability — instead of manually executing transactions in a console, use an automated script so other developers can reproduce your steps. A common misconception is that scripts are only for deployment; they can also run migrations, set initial state, or help with local testing. When you write scripts, avoid hardcoding real private keys. Use environment variables or placeholders for accounts. The main benefit is working reproducibly: if the script reliably deploys Greeter in your environment, teammates can run the same script and get consistent results. The scripts/ directory and deploy workflow means store deployment and utility scripts in scripts/ to run consistent, reproducible workflows across environments.. screens.title: The test/ directory and testing workflow
screens.subtitle: Write unit and integration tests using JavaScript/TypeScript

narration.text: The test directory is where you author automated tests for your smart contracts. Hardhat integrates with test runners like Mocha and assertion libraries such as Chai so you can write readable tests in JavaScript or TypeScript. The sample project includes Greeter. js as a starting point. In tests you instantiate contract instances, call functions, and assert expected state changes or emitted events. A concrete example: a test might deploy Greeter, call greet(), and assert that the returned string matches the expected text. Tests are essential for security because contracts are immutable once deployed; a failing test before deployment often catches logic or access-control errors. A common misconception is relying only on manual checks — automated tests scale and document intended behavior. Use test files to validate edge cases, revert conditions, and typical user flows. Keep test code under version control and make them fast and deterministic by using Hardhat Network and snapshots to reset state between test cases. screens.title: hardhat.config.js — the central configuration
screens.subtitle: How compiler, networks, and plugins are defined

narration.text: hardhat. config. js is the central configuration file that shapes how Hardhat compiles, tests, and deploys your project. In this file you declare which Solidity compiler version to use, optimizer settings, network endpoints and accounts, and any plugins you want to load. This single file ensures everyone on the team compiles contracts with the same settings. A common practical action is specifying the solidity version so it aligns with your contracts' pragma directives. If the configured version doesn't match the source, compilation errors or incompatibilities will occur. Another role of this file is registering network endpoints: you can define a local Hardhat Network for development and placeholders for testnets. You can also add custom tasks or plugin configurations here. The mental model is simple: hardhat. config. js tells the toolchain how to interpret and build your project, so treat it like the project's environment manifest. hardhat.config.js — the central configuration means use hardhat.config.js to set compiler versions, networks, optimizer settings, and plugins so builds are consistent across machines.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Definition hardhat.config.js
hardhat.config.js — the central configuration
Define compilers, networks, and plugins in one place to ensure reproducible builds.
What it configures
  • Solidity compiler version and optimizer settings.
  • Network endpoints and accounts for deployment targets.
  • Plugins and custom Hardhat tasks.
Treat this file as your environment manifest. Keep it under version control so teammates share the same build settings.
Misconception
Some developers edit compiler settings without checking contract pragmas. Always ensure the configured Solidity version is compatible with your sources to avoid build failures.
Why it matters
A mismatched compiler setting can block compilation and delay deployments, especially when optimizer runs affect bytecode size and gas characteristics.

screens.title: hardhat.config.js — example and explanation
screens.subtitle: Read and interpret a basic configuration snippet

narration.text: Let's walk through a minimal hardhat. config. js example to see concrete settings. The example begins by requiring the toolbox plugin, which bundles helpful utilities. Next the module exports an object that sets the solidity property to a specific compiler version. That line tells Hardhat which compiler to invoke. The networks object includes a local hardhat network configuration with a chainId, and an example testnet configuration with a URL and accounts. The testnet entry uses a placeholder for an RPC endpoint and references process environment variables for private keys — never commit real keys. The solidity version, chain identifiers, and accounts are the main things that influence compilation and deployment behavior. If you change the solidity version here, you should verify your contracts’ pragma statements remain compatible. content.html:
Code Walkthrough hardhat.config.js example
hardhat.config.js — example and explanation
A small configuration that sets the compiler and networks.
// hardhat.config.js
require("@nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox");

/** @type import('hardhat/config').HardhatUserConfig */
module.exports = {
  solidity: "0.8.19", // Specify the Solidity compiler version
  networks: {
    hardhat: {
      // Configuration for the Hardhat Network (local development)
      chainId: 31337, // Default Hardhat Network chain ID
    },
    sepolia: {
      url: "https://sepolia.infura.io/v3/YOUR_INFURA_API_KEY", // Example for Sepolia testnet
      accounts: [process.env.PRIVATE_KEY] // Accounts for deployment
    }
  }
};
Annotated highlights
  • require loads plugins that extend Hardhat with utilities.
  • solidity selects the compiler version; keep it compatible with contract pragmas.
  • networks lists deployment targets; use environment variables for secrets.
Misconception
Changing the compiler here automatically changes pragma lines in contracts. It does not. Verify compatibility explicitly in source files.

narration.text: package. json is the Node. js manifest that lists your project name, scripts, dependencies, and devDependencies. Hardhat and its plugins are listed here so npm can install them. package-lock. json records the exact package versions installed, including nested dependencies. This lockfile ensures that when a teammate runs npm install they get the same dependency tree, which helps avoid subtle "works on my machine" problems. A concrete workflow: after running npm init -y and installing Hardhat, you will see hardhat and related packages in package. json. Commit both package. json and package-lock. json to version control. A common mistake is committing node_modules instead of relying on package-lock. json; node_modules is large and environment-specific. The correct practice is to include package-lock. json, ignore node_modules via. gitignore, and let npm reconstruct the module tree deterministically. This pattern makes onboarding faster and builds reproducible across CI and developer machines. package.json and package-lock.json means keep package.json and package-lock.json under version control so teammates can reproduce the exact dependency tree.. In practical terms, dependency management and deterministic installs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lock your dependencies
keyIdea.text: Keep package.json and package-lock.json under version control so teammates can reproduce the exact dependency tree.

content.html:
Core Files package.json & package-lock.json
package.json and package-lock.json
Manage dependencies and ensure deterministic installs across machines.
package.json
Lists project metadata and dependency ranges. Developers and CI use its scripts and dependency declarations to install and run tooling.
Why commit it?
So collaborators know which packages the project needs and how to run npm scripts like test or compile.
package-lock.json
Records exact package versions installed, including nested dependencies, making installs reproducible.
Common mistake
Not committing the lockfile can lead to different dependency resolutions between developers or CI systems.
Key Takeaway
Commit package.json and package-lock.json; ignore node_modules to keep repo size manageable and installs deterministic.

screens.title: node_modules/ and .gitignore
screens.subtitle: Why node_modules is excluded from version control

narration.text: node_modules is the folder where npm installs all package code. It can be very large and contains platform-specific artifacts. Because of its size and machine-specific contents, node_modules should never be committed to Git. Instead, include package. json and package-lock. json and add node_modules/ to. gitignore. This keeps repositories small and ensures each developer builds their own node_modules from the lockfile. A common error is accidentally committing node_modules or build cache directories like cache/; this bloats the repo and can create merge conflicts. If node_modules is accidentally committed, remove it, add it to. gitignore, and commit the change. The correct workflow for team projects is to share the manifest and lockfile and let developers run npm install locally or in CI to reconstruct node_modules deterministically. This practice keeps version control focused on source and configuration, not installed libraries. node_modules/ and .gitignore means do not commit node_modules; use .gitignore and rely on package-lock.json for reproducible installs.. In practical terms, why node_modules is excluded from version control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ignore installed packages
keyIdea.text: Do not commit node_modules; use .gitignore and rely on package-lock.json for reproducible installs.

content.html:
Directory node_modules/ and .gitignore
node_modules/ and .gitignore
Installed dependencies are restored from lockfiles rather than stored in Git.
Why not commit node_modules?
  • It's large and bloats your repository.
  • It contains platform-specific files that differ across systems.
  • It defeats the purpose of package-lock determinism.
Best practice
Add node_modules/ to .gitignore and commit package-lock.json so others can run npm install to recreate the same modules.
Common mistake
Forgetting .gitignore entries and accidentally committing cache/ or node_modules/ will create repository bloat and collaboration issues.

screens.title: cache/ and artifacts/ — compilation outputs
screens.subtitle: What gets generated and why you typically don't commit it

narration.text: When you compile your contracts with Hardhat, it generates two major directories: cache and artifacts. cache stores internal compilation caches that speed up subsequent builds. You can delete it safely; Hardhat will regenerate it. artifacts is more important for integration: it contains the compiled outputs for each contract, usually as JSON files that include metadata, the ABI, and bytecode. For example, after compiling Greeter. sol you will find Greeter. json under artifacts with the contract’s ABI and its EVM bytecode. The ABI describes the contract interface and is used by frontend applications and scripts to call contract functions. Bytecode is the compiled machine code that the EVM executes. A common practice is not to commit artifacts or cache since they can be regenerated; instead, share source and let downstream build steps produce artifacts as needed. If you need to share an ABI with a frontend, consider copying the ABI into a curated interface folder or exporting it during CI rather than committing the full artifacts folder. cache/ and artifacts/ — compilation outputs means artifacts are generated outputs used by frontends and scripts; they include the abi and bytecode produced by compilation.. In practical terms, what gets generated and why you typically don't commit it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Artifacts contain ABI & bytecode

content.html:
Output cache/ and artifacts/

Generated files that connect compiled contracts to deployments and frontends.
cache/

artifacts/

screens.title: What an artifact contains — ABI and bytecode
screens.subtitle: How frontends and scripts use artifacts to interact with contracts

narration.text: Artifacts are JSON files produced by compilation that package everything needed to interact with a contract. At minimum they include the ABI — a JSON description of the contract’s functions, events, and argument types — and the bytecode that the EVM executes when deploying a contract. Frontend applications use the ABI to construct contract calls and encode parameters. Deployment scripts use bytecode when creating a new contract instance on-chain. For example, Greeter. json will include a field labeled abi describing the contract interface and a bytecode field containing the compiled machine code. A common misconception is treating ABI as executable code; it is not — ABI is a description of how to call functions, not the implementation. When integrating, pull the ABI into your frontend or packaging step, and rely on artifacts generated by CI for canonical ABIs rather than copying hand-typed interfaces. The point is this: artifacts translate source code into the pieces other systems need to interact safely and predictably with your contracts. What an artifact contains — ABI and bytecode means abi describes callable functions and events; bytecode is the compiled deployable code. both are produced into artifacts json files.. In practical terms, how frontends and scripts use artifacts to interact with contracts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Organizing a growing project
screens.subtitle: Subdirectories, naming, and what to commit

narration.text: As projects grow, maintainability depends on a clear organization strategy. For contracts, use subdirectories like contracts/tokens or contracts/governance so related contracts live together. For scripts, group deployment scripts by network or feature, for example scripts/deploy/mainnet and scripts/deploy/testnet, or scripts/setup to initialize state. Keep tests mirrored to the structure of contracts so developers can find tests for a specific contract quickly. When deciding what to commit, include source files and lockfiles but exclude generated outputs and installed modules. A practical approach is to commit a curated ABI folder if your frontend needs stable interfaces — produce those ABIs from CI rather than committing full artifacts. A common misconception is keeping everything in a single flat folder because it's simpler; this works only for tiny projects and becomes chaotic quickly. Naming conventions matter too: choose consistent prefixes or names and document them in a README so new contributors understand where to add code. Clear organization reduces onboarding time and makes code reviews faster. Organizing a growing project means use subfolders and consistent naming conventions so the project stays navigable as it grows.. In practical terms, subdirectories, naming, and what to commit. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Pitfalls and how to avoid them
screens.subtitle: Common errors: editing node_modules, ignoring .gitignore, and version mismatches

narration.text: Several recurring mistakes slow Hardhat projects down. One is editing node_modules directly. Because node_modules contains third-party package code, changes there are fragile and will be overwritten by installs; if you need to change a dependency, fork it and link or publish a patched version instead. Another common issue is forgetting to include node_modules or cache in. gitignore, which leads to oversized repositories and merge headaches. Misplacing contract files outside contracts/ without updating paths in hardhat. config. js can also break the compiler pipeline. Perhaps the most frequent runtime problem is mismatched Solidity versions: if your contracts declare a pragma that doesn’t fall within the configured compiler version in hardhat. config. js, compilation will fail or produce unexpected results. The remedy is to check pragmas, set compatible compiler ranges, and keep configuration and source aligned. Finally, don't commit generated artifacts; instead, produce them in CI and distribute selected ABIs if needed. These practices keep your project maintainable and predictable for teammates. Pitfalls and how to avoid them means never edit node_modules; maintain .gitignore and ensure pragma/solidity settings match to avoid compilation failures.. In practical terms, common errors: editing node_modules, ignoring .gitignore, and version mismatches. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
